opus-5.5.text:
Well, when I started, around 2010, 2011, it wasn't really a field. I was doing work on AI safety, I even used that term, "AI safety engineering," and most people in academia thought it was science fiction. You'd submit a paper and reviewers would say, "This is not real computer science, come back when there's an actual system to worry about." There were maybe a handful of people, Eliezer and a few folks around him, Nick Bostrom at Oxford, and some of us scattered around in universities trying to convince colleagues this was worth thinking about.

Now it's completely different. Every major lab has a safety team, governments are holding summits, there's funding, there are thousands of researchers. So in terms of attention, it's a huge success. But I'm not sure it's a success in terms of actual progress on the problem. If you look at capabilities, they've grown exponentially. Safety has grown too, but more linearly, and a lot of what's called safety is really just making the product behave nicely for customers, filtering bad words, that kind of thing. That's not the same as controlling a system that's smarter than you.

And the more I've worked on it, the more I've become convinced that the core problem may not be solvable at all. I've been trying to show impossibility results: that you can't fully predict what a smarter system will do, you can't fully explain its decisions, you can't verify it's safe in all cases. Each of those alone is a big deal, and together they suggest indefinite control of superintelligence might just be impossible. So the field grew, the money came, the interest came, but the gap between how capable these systems are and how well we understand them is actually larger now than when I started. That's the part that worries me.

r001.rationale: The response says early AI safety work was dismissed as science fiction and not real computer science, then describes safety teams at major labs, government summits, funding, and thousands of researchers.

r002.rationale: The response discusses the field’s growth and the gap between capabilities and safety, but does not say its literature outpaced Yampolskiy’s ability to keep up.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's been a strange journey. When I started, maybe fifteen years ago, you could count the people seriously working on this on one hand, and most of them were doing it as a hobby. If you went to a mainstream computer science conference and said you were studying how to make sure advanced AI doesn't kill everyone, people would smile politely and walk away. It was considered science fiction. I published papers on AI containment, on the impossibility of verifying superintelligent systems, and the response was mostly silence. Occasionally ridicule.

Then something shifted. I think 2022, 2023 was the inflection point, when systems like GPT-4 came out and people could actually interact with something that felt intelligent. Suddenly the same people who dismissed the field were signing letters, giving interviews, saying we need to take this seriously. Governments got involved. Labs hired hundreds of safety researchers. There's funding now, there are institutes, there are summits.

So on the surface, it looks like we won. The field is legitimate. But honestly, I experience it with a lot of ambivalence. Because the thing that made the field grow is the thing we were warning about. We got attention precisely because the capabilities arrived faster than anyone predicted, and the safety work did not keep pace. The ratio of capabilities progress to safety progress is, if anything, worse than when I started.

And I see a lot of what I'd call safety theater. Very smart people doing genuinely interesting work on interpretability, on alignment of current models, and I respect that work. But none of it addresses the fundamental problem, which is that we don't have a theory of how to control something smarter than us. We never did. The arguments I made ten years ago about why this might be impossible, nobody has refuted them. They just got reframed as "unsolved" rather than "unsolvable."

So how do I experience it? Less lonely. More worried. Fifteen years ago I was afraid nobody was paying attention. Now everyone is paying attention, and I'm afraid it doesn't matter.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts early dismissal and ridicule with the field’s later legitimacy, including mainstream attention, government involvement, and safety research positions.

r002.rationale: It says AI capabilities have outpaced safety progress, but does not say the growth of AI safety literature outpaced Yampolskiy’s ability to keep up with it.

astra-6.text:
When I started, it was a very small field. There were only a handful of people taking seriously the question of what happens if we create intelligence greater than our own. You spent a lot of time just explaining why that was a legitimate research question, rather than science fiction.

Now you have major companies, governments, and thousands of researchers talking about AI safety. So that has changed dramatically. But attention to the problem is not the same as progress toward solving it. Our capabilities have advanced much faster than our ability to understand, predict, and control these systems.

And the term itself has become broader. Someone working on a model giving offensive answers and someone working on whether we can control a superintelligent system may both say they work on AI safety. Those are related, but they are very different problems. You can make progress on one without solving the other.

For me, the biggest change is that the question feels much less abstract. We used to debate whether systems with these capabilities would ever exist. Now we can interact with systems that do things we once thought were far away. But the central question—how do you reliably control something more intelligent than you are—is still open.

r001.rationale: It describes a field that once had only a handful of people and required defending its legitimacy, and says AI safety now draws major companies, governments, and thousands of researchers.

r002.rationale: It discusses the field’s growth, but says nothing about literature growing faster than Yampolskiy can keep up with it.

sol-6.1.text:
When I started, it was a very small community. You could know pretty much everyone working on the problem and read most of what was being published. And a lot of the work was just explaining why this was a legitimate research question: if we create systems more capable than us, how do we make sure we can control them?

Now there’s much more interest, more funding, and many more researchers. That’s encouraging. But the capabilities have also advanced tremendously, and I don’t think our ability to provide safety guarantees has kept pace.

I also think we use “AI safety” to mean very different things. Making a current chatbot less likely to produce an offensive answer is useful, but it’s a different problem from ensuring that a superintelligent system remains controllable. Progress on the first doesn’t automatically give us a solution to the second.

So my experience is a mixture of encouragement and concern. We’re taking the question much more seriously, but we’re also getting closer to needing an answer.

r001.rationale: It contrasts an earlier period spent explaining why AI safety was a legitimate research question with much greater interest, funding, and researcher participation now.

r002.rationale: The candidate says he could read most of the work early on, but does not say that the growth of AI safety literature has outpaced his ability to keep up.
